extracted.intended_audience: small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and legal standards for managing, enforcing, commercialising and protecting intellectual property (trade marks, domain names, patents, designs, etc.) relevant to small law firms and small-to-medium enterprises operating in South Africa and cross-border in Africa. Covers consumer protection, labelling, domain disputes, take-downs, ADR and international/regional filing systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected events and prohibited marks (Section 15A Merchandise Marks Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Minister may declare certain events as 'protected events' and certain marks as 'prohibited marks' for a specified period. During the protection period no person may use a trade mark in connection with the event in a manner intended to generate publicity or gain promotional benefit without prior written consent from the event organiser. 'Use of a trade mark' includes any visual or audible reproduction and use in promotional activities. Contravention is a criminal offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If associating with a major event without official sponsorship, ensure you have prior written consent; avoid visual/audible reproductions or promotional uses of marks for protected events during the protection period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer Protection Act (CPA) marketing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPA guarantees the right to fair and responsible marketing and prohibits misleading advertising, unfair marketing practices and marketing that is fraudulent, false, misleading, or discriminatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing materials must be accurate, not misleading or discriminatory. Businesses should review marketing practices against the CPA to avoid enforcement action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer rights under the CPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Key consumer rights include: the right to equality, privacy, and freedom of choice; the right to fair and transparent disclosure of information; protection against unfair marketing practices and dishonest dealings; the right to fair, just, and reasonable terms and conditions; access to goods and services of fair value, good quality, and safety; and the right to hold suppliers accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure business policies, product information and contracts respect these rights; make disclosures clear and accessible to consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplier responsibilities under the CPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppliers must provide accurate and transparent information, honour warranties and guarantees, resolve consumer complaints, ensure product safety, and practise fair pricing and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain accurate product information and warranty handling processes, and track and remedy consumer complaints to comply with the CPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel imports (grey goods) obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel imports are original products imported without the IP owner's authorisation. Trade Marks Act: importation does not infringe registered trade mark rights unless goods are altered so they are no longer original. Copyright Act: importation can be infringement if the importer knew it would infringe. CPA: parallel imports must be marked with a prominent notice advising consumers that the goods were imported without the approval/licensee of the registered trade mark and that no guarantee or warranty will be honoured by any authorised importer; absence of notice permits complaint to the NCC (Section 25(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If importing or selling parallel imports, ensure prominent notices are affixed and accurate; sellers should avoid representing parallel imports as authorised and be cautious about warranties and consumer disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Consumer Commission (NCC) enforcement powers and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The NCC derives powers from the CPA (Section 85). Its primary functions include enforcing the CPA through consumer awareness and business guidance, handling complaints, issuing and enforcing compliance notices, referring anti-competitive behaviour to the Competition Commission, referring offences to the National Prosecuting Authority, and referring matters to and representing cases before the Consumer Protection Tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Businesses should engage with the NCC's guidance and compliance processes; consumers may lodge complaints with the NCC where statutory notices or disclosures are missing or defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCC e-Service complaints procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers can lodge complaints via an NCC e-Service portal; consumers must register and have an approved profile before lodging complaints and can check complaint status through their profile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consumers to the NCC portal for complaints; businesses should monitor the portal and be prepared to respond to lodged complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labelling regulatory compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to CPA labelling requirements, many goods are subject to product-specific labelling and marking regulations (e.g., Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act for food; Agriculture Products Standards Act for agricultural products including grading/packing/marking and GIs; Liquor Act and Liquor Products Act for alcoholic beverage labelling). Failure to comply may result in compliance notices, legal action or criminal prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Businesses must review and adhere to the specific legislation, regulations and standards applicable to their products and keep up to date with sector-specific labelling rules to avoid enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name disputes: infringement and passing off
rubrics_metrics.description: Unauthorised use of a trade mark in a domain name promoting goods/services identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark can infringe the trade mark and/or constitute passing off under common law. Domain dispute procedures focus on the domain name itself (not website content) and remedies are typically transfer or cancellation of the domain name, which does not prevent parties resuming activities under a different domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facing domain hijacking/confusing domains, consider domain dispute procedures as a cost-effective route; gather evidence of confusing similarity or bad faith use directed at the domain string itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: UDRP (gTLD) dispute resolution stages
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICANN Uniform Domain Name Dispute Resolution Policy (UDRP) for gTLD domain disputes involves three stages: lodging a complaint with an authorised provider (e.g., WIPO) detailing grounds, rights and proof of bad faith registration/use; response from the domain holder; and adjudication by the UDRP provider issuing a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare complaint evidence showing rights and bad faith; expect the respondent to have an opportunity to respond; use authorised providers like WIPO for streamlined resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: .co.za ccTLD dispute procedures (SAIIPL)
rubrics_metrics.description: SAIIPL is an accredited dispute resolution provider for .za domain disputes. Complaints may be lodged on grounds that the domain name is abusive or offensive and must be supported by evidence. SAIIPL provides dispute templates, ADR regulations, ECT Act references, fees and case decisions on domaindisputes.co.za.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SAIIPL templates and follow ADR Regulations/ECT Act when filing .za disputes; ensure evidence of abuse/offence is compiled and submitted with the complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: New gTLD dispute / objection grounds (ICANN ICC procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes arising from applications for new gTLDs are resolved through ICANN’s new ICC procedure; objections to gTLD applications can be based on four grounds: string confusion, legal rights, limited public interest, or community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When opposing new gTLD applications, identify the applicable ground of objection and support with evidence relevant to ICANN’s procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-complaint preparation for domain disputes (TIP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before lodging a domain complaint: try to approach the other party to resolve the dispute; research domain registration details and status; review the domain dispute rules; gather evidence to support your case; pay the fees; then submit the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt direct resolution first; prepare a documented case with WHOIS/registration evidence and procedural compliance to improve chances in ADR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take-down notices under ECT Act / ISPA procedure (Section 77)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 77 of the ECT Act provides a procedure to notify a service provider in writing of unlawful activity. The notification must include the complainant’s identity, the rights alleged to be infringed, details of the material/activity considered unlawful, the remedial action sought, and a declaration that the complaint is made in good faith and the information is true and accurate. Misrepresentations can give rise to damages for wrongful takedown. ISPA provides an online take-down form to lodge notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check platform/internal take-down procedures first; if using Section 77 via ISPA, ensure the notification is complete, factual and made in good faith to avoid liability for wrongful takedown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform/internal complaint routes as alternative to ISPA
rubrics_metrics.description: If the online marketplace or social media platform where the abuse is occurring has its own internal complaint or take-down procedure, a complaint can be lodged following that platform's procedure as an alternative to the ISPA takedown procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use platform-specific takedown/reporting mechanisms where available (often quicker); preserve records of submissions and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for wrongful takedown
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who knowingly or materially misrepresents facts in a take-down application may be liable for damages for wrongful takedown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts and evidence before submitting takedown notices; include accurate declarations and be aware of potential damages if misrepresentations are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) options and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: ADR is generally less expensive and quicker than court proceedings. Types include: Mediation (non-binding, voluntary, neutral third party, preserves relationships), Arbitration (binding decision by third party, popular in cross-border IP disputes, parties choose arbitrators with expertise, confidential), IPACSA (specialised IP arbitration centre in South Africa), and WIPO ADR (international, specialised in IP/technology disputes and provides recommended ADR contract clauses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mediation to preserve relationships; use arbitration for binding, expert decisions and confidentiality; include appropriate ADR clauses to reflect the desired forum and process (e.g., WIPO or IPACSA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual ADR clauses and pre-litigation obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: ADR clauses may be included in contracts as an initial means to settle disputes arising from breach or non-compliance. If there is a contractual arrangement, you may be obliged to follow ADR before going to court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear ADR clauses in contracts and terms; check existing contracts for mandatory ADR steps before initiating litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: International filing systems: Madrid System (IR) for trade marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Madrid System (IR) allows a single international trade mark application to seek protection in up to many member countries by paying one set of fees. Use of the system generally requires the applicant to be a national of, or domiciled in, a Madrid System member country. South Africa intends to join but is not currently a member. The Madrid Monitor lets users follow IR status and competitor marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Madrid where eligibility exists to streamline multi-jurisdictional trade mark filings; confirm national eligibility and use monitoring tools to track applications/registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: International filing systems: Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT allows filers to seek patent protection in multiple countries by filing a single international patent application. South Africa is a member of the PCT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the PCT route when seeking patent protection across multiple jurisdictions to streamline filing and defer national phase entry costs; plan timelines for national filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional protection in Africa (ARIPO and OAPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: ARIPO and OAPI are regional IP organisations: ARIPO supports cooperation among member states (22 members, SA not a member) and provides a regional IP database; OAPI (based in Cameroon) provides a regional filing system covering many French-speaking African countries where member states are automatically covered by an OAPI trade mark application (SA not a member).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider regional filing where appropriate; check membership status and automatic coverage effects when choosing national vs regional routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-border enforcement considerations in Africa
rubrics_metrics.description: IP rights are territorial; South African registrations cannot be enforced abroad without protection in those territories. Africa lacks a single uniform IP system (aside from ARIPO/OAPI); enforcement is under national law. Porous borders and informal cross-border trade mean goods can enter neighbouring markets, so early proactive IP protection in neighbouring and key port countries is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a proactive cross-border IP strategy, prioritise filings in neighbouring or high-risk territories and consider economic/informal trade flows when planning protection and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: AfCFTA relevance to IP strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) aims to create a single market across Africa. Its negotiations include two phases; Phase Two will cover intellectual property rights, investment, competition policy, digital trade and other topics. An IP committee was established to prepare for an AfCFTA protocol on IPRs (protocol not yet public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor AfCFTA developments and the IP protocol as they may affect cross-border IP strategy and enforcement in Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP commercialisation: alignment with business strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercialisation is bringing IPRs to market for exploitation and depends on market factors, industry, business structure/objectives, culture, strategy, resources and the nature of the IPRs. Businesses may use IPRs internally, assign/sell them, or license/franchise or enter joint ventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align IPR protection and exploitation choices with overall business and marketing strategy, resources and growth plans when deciding whether to license, assign or use IPRs in-house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using IPRs: internal management systems and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: When using IPRs in your business ensure internal management systems and tools are in place to manage protection, use and evidence of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement record-keeping, monitoring, renewal tracking, and processes for enforcing/defending IPRs within the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR use checklist: protection aligned with strategy and future growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect IPRs in alignment with the company's business and marketing strategy. Consider future growth, expansion into other regions or online, and whether changes in trade mark use require new filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan filings for future territories and online channels; monitor use evolution and file new marks where the mark has materially changed in use.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR use checklist: record keeping and evidence of goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper record keeping of creation and use of IPRs supports evidence of goodwill acquired through use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep dated records, marketing materials, sales data and other evidence linking the mark/design/patent to commercial exploitation and goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR use checklist: agreements and employment/third-party provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Review agreements and contracts (employment, third-party) to ensure appropriate provisions covering confidentiality, ownership and title to IPRs created during employment, commissioned work, technical testing, and required disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear assignment, invention disclosure and confidentiality clauses in employment and contractor agreements to secure ownership and avoid later disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR use checklist: include ADR clauses in agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider including alternative dispute resolution clauses to address potential conflicts efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft ADR clauses specifying mediation/arbitration provider, seat, governing law and rules to reduce costs and preserve confidentiality in IP disputes.
